subject: computing
title: KS3 Computing — Internet, Protocols & the World Wide Web
subtitle: How the internet works, key protocols, DNS, packet switching, and HTTP vs HTTPS.

data.targetWord: The global physical and logical infrastructure — the worldwide network of interconnected networks consisting of cables, routers, servers, and billions of connected devices

examples.en-GB: The internet is like the road network — the physical infrastructure that carries traffic; the World Wide Web is just one of many services that travel on it.

data.targetWord: A service that runs on top of the internet, consisting of linked web pages accessed via a browser using the HTTP or HTTPS protocol — it is not the same as the internet itself

examples.en-GB: When you browse a website with a browser, you are using the World Wide Web — but the internet also carries email, video streaming, and gaming.

data.targetWord: A unique numerical identifier assigned to every device on a network, used by routers to direct data packets to the correct destination

examples.en-GB: An IP address such as 192.168.1.1 works like a postal address, telling routers exactly where to deliver each data packet.

data.targetWord: Internet Protocol version 4 — the original IP address format using 32 bits, written as four groups of numbers (e.g. 192.168.1.1), providing approximately 4.3 billion unique addresses

examples.en-GB: IPv4 addresses have nearly all been used up because there are more internet-connected devices than the 4.3 billion IPv4 addresses can accommodate.

data.targetWord: Internet Protocol version 6 — the replacement for IPv4, using 128 bits to provide approximately 340 undecillion unique addresses, developed to solve IPv4 address exhaustion

examples.en-GB: IPv6 addresses look like 2001:0db8:85a3::8a2e:0370:7334 and provide so many unique addresses that every device on Earth could have billions of them.

data.targetWord: Domain Name System — the system that translates human-readable domain names (such as www.bbc.co.uk) into IP addresses that computers use to find servers

examples.en-GB: DNS works like a phone book for the internet — you look up a name and it gives you the number (IP address) you need to make a connection.

data.targetWord: A human-readable address for a website or server on the internet, such as www.bbc.co.uk, which DNS translates into an IP address

examples.en-GB: Domain names like www.google.com are much easier to remember than the numerical IP address 142.250.187.78.

data.targetWord: A small chunk that data is divided into before being sent across a network; each packet contains a header with source and destination IP addresses, a sequence number, a payload of actual data, and a trailer for error checking

examples.en-GB: A large file is split into thousands of packets; each packet travels independently across the network and is reassembled at the destination.

data.targetWord: The method used to send data across the internet, where data is broken into packets that may each take different routes to the destination and are then reassembled in the correct order

examples.en-GB: Packet switching is efficient because it shares network infrastructure — if one route is busy or broken, packets automatically find alternative paths.

data.targetWord: HyperText Transfer Protocol — the protocol used to transfer web pages from a server to a browser; data is sent as unencrypted plain text

examples.en-GB: HTTP sends data as plain text, so anyone intercepting the connection could read the information — which is why HTTPS should be used for sensitive websites.

data.targetWord: HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure — HTTP with SSL/TLS encryption added, so data is encrypted in transit and cannot be read by anyone intercepting it

examples.en-GB: Banking and shopping websites must use HTTPS to protect customers' financial details; a padlock icon in the browser confirms the connection is encrypted.

data.targetWord: The combined protocol suite that forms the foundation of internet communication: TCP splits data into packets and ensures reliable delivery, while IP handles routing packets across networks

examples.en-GB: TCP/IP is the core protocol of the internet — TCP ensures every packet arrives and is reassembled correctly, while IP tells routers where to send each packet.

data.targetWord: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol — the protocol used for sending email from a client to a mail server, or between mail servers

examples.en-GB: When you click Send in your email app, SMTP is the protocol that transmits the email from your device to the mail server.

data.targetWord: Internet Message Access Protocol — a protocol for receiving email where messages remain stored on the server, allowing access from multiple devices

examples.en-GB: IMAP is used by most modern email services because your inbox is stored on the server, so you can read the same emails on your phone, laptop, and tablet.

data.targetWord: File Transfer Protocol — a protocol for transferring files between computers over a network, commonly used to upload files to a web server

examples.en-GB: Web developers use FTP to upload their HTML and image files from their computer to the web server that hosts their website.

data.targetWord: A set of agreed rules that defines how data is formatted, transmitted, and received, allowing different devices and software to communicate reliably

examples.en-GB: Without protocols, a Windows computer and a Mac would not know how to exchange data, because they would each use different formats and rules.

data.targetWord: Secure Sockets Layer / Transport Layer Security — encryption protocols used by HTTPS to encrypt data in transit between a browser and a web server

examples.en-GB: TLS replaced the older SSL protocol but both are commonly referred to as SSL; they scramble data so interceptors see only meaningless ciphertext.

data.targetWord: Uniform Resource Locator — the full web address used to access a specific resource on the internet, such as https://www.bbc.co.uk/news

examples.en-GB: A URL includes the protocol (https://), the domain name (www.bbc.co.uk), and the specific path (/news) to locate an exact resource.

data.targetWord: A program used to access and display web pages from the World Wide Web by making HTTP/HTTPS requests to web servers

examples.en-GB: Chrome, Firefox, and Safari are web browsers — they send HTTP requests to web servers and render the HTML responses as visible web pages.

data.targetWord: A computer that stores web pages and serves them to browsers in response to HTTP/HTTPS requests

examples.en-GB: When you type a URL, your browser sends an HTTP request to the web server, which responds by sending back the HTML and images of the requested page.

data.targetWord: A clickable link in a web page that connects to another web page or resource, allowing users to navigate between pages on the World Wide Web

examples.en-GB: Hyperlinks are what makes the World Wide Web a 'web' — clicking a hyperlink takes you from one page to a related resource anywhere on the internet.

data.targetWord: HyperText Markup Language — the standard language used to create and structure web pages, defining headings, paragraphs, links, and images

examples.en-GB: When your browser receives a web page, it receives HTML code that it interprets to display text, images, and hyperlinks as a formatted page.

data.targetWord: The process of scrambling data into an unreadable format using a key, so that only the intended recipient with the correct key can decode and read it

examples.en-GB: HTTPS uses encryption so that even if a hacker intercepts your data, they see only scrambled text that is meaningless without the decryption key.

data.targetWord: The first section of a data packet, containing control information such as the source IP address, destination IP address, and sequence number

examples.en-GB: Routers read each packet's header to find the destination IP address and decide which route the packet should take next.

data.targetWord: The section of a data packet that contains the actual data being transmitted — for example, a portion of a web page or file

examples.en-GB: The payload is the useful content of a packet; the header and trailer are the control information that surrounds it.

data.targetWord: The final section of a data packet, containing error-checking information (a checksum) used to verify that the packet arrived without corruption

examples.en-GB: If the checksum in the trailer does not match the received data, the receiving device knows the packet was corrupted and requests it to be resent.

data.targetWord: A network device that reads the destination IP address of each incoming packet and forwards it toward its destination, connecting networks together

examples.en-GB: Internet packets pass through many routers on their journey — each router makes an independent decision about where to send the packet next.

data.targetWord: Internet Service Provider — a company that provides customers with access to the internet, acting as the connection between a home or office network and the wider internet

examples.en-GB: Your ISP provides the broadband connection that links your home router to the internet infrastructure.

data.targetWord: Remote servers accessible over the internet that store, manage, and process data, allowing users to access files and run applications without local hardware

examples.en-GB: Cloud storage services like Google Drive store your files on internet servers so you can access them from any device anywhere in the world.

data.targetWord: A number in each packet's header that records its position in the original message, allowing the receiving device to reassemble packets in the correct order

examples.en-GB: Because packets may arrive out of order, the sequence number tells the destination device how to reassemble them into the original message.

data.title: Typing a URL to Seeing a Web Page
data.instruction: Put these steps in the correct order to describe what happens from a user typing a URL to the web page appearing on screen.
items: User types www.example.com into the browser
Browser checks its local DNS cache for the IP address
Browser sends a DNS query to the DNS server
DNS server returns the IP address to the browser
Browser sends an HTTP request to the web server at that IP address
Web server responds by sending HTML, CSS, and image packets
Packets are reassembled at the destination
Browser renders the page and displays it to the user

data.title: How DNS Resolves a Domain Name
data.instruction: Arrange these steps in the correct order to show how DNS resolves a domain name.
items: User types a domain name into the browser
Browser checks its local cache — is the IP address already stored?
If not cached, browser sends a DNS query to the DNS server
DNS server looks up the domain name in its records
DNS server returns the corresponding IP address
Browser uses the IP address to contact the web server
